quizzes.title: Origin and Objective: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage: Changing parties after being elected has long been a concern in Indian politics. An old expression, often quoted in this context, describes members who switched their political loyalties again and again, and it is linked to a period of frequent shifts among legislators. The rules that address this problem form part of the Constitution. They sit in a dedicated schedule, which groups the provisions on the subject together. These rules were brought in through a constitutional amendment, so they were added to the Constitution rather than passed as an ordinary statute. Two officers play a central role when a complaint is raised under them: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Their decisions matter because they determine whether a member keeps a seat. The booklet also records that these decisions have been the subject of concern for some time. The subject has also been examined in several Supreme Court judgments, which the booklet lists in its discussion of the topic. Those judgments deal with the powers of presiding officers and the extent to which courts may review their decisions. Taken together, the origin of the rules, their place in the Constitution, and the officers who apply them form the basic background for understanding how the framework works in practice.

questions.q: The phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' is linked to frequent party-switching by legislators in which decade?
questions.explanation: The booklet links the phrase to frequent party-switching by legislators in the 1960s.

questions.q: To which legislatures does the Anti-Defection Law apply?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the law applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures.

questions.q: Through which Constitutional Amendment Act was the Anti-Defection Law introduced?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Party stability is one of the aims of the Anti-Defection Law.
Reason (R): The law aims to prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The stated objective of the law is to prevent political defections and ensure stability in governments, which is the reason for the aim in A.

questions.q: What does the Anti-Defection Law lay down?
options: The process by which legislators may be disqualified on grounds of defection
The procedure for electing the Speaker
The number of members needed to form a government
The salaries payable to presiding officers
questions.explanation: The booklet says the law lays down the process by which legislators may be disqualified on the grounds of defection.

questions.q:
Read the following statements:
I. The phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' is linked to party-switching in the 1960s.
II. The law was introduced through the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
III. The law applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III match the booklet, while the law was introduced through the 52nd Amendment, not the 91st.

questions.q:
Based on the booklet, how many of the following statements are correct?
I. The law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
II. The law applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures.
III. The phrase 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' is linked to party-switching in the 1970s.
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the phrase is linked to the 1960s, not the 1970s.

quizzes.title: Grounds for Disqualification: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage: A legislator does not lose membership simply because he or she disagrees with a colleague or a party leader. The rules on loss of membership are set out as a list of specific grounds, and the list covers both a member's conduct and his or her personal circumstances. Some grounds relate to choices a member makes in connection with a political party. Others relate to the member's status and to certain personal circumstances. Decisions on these grounds are made by the presiding officer of the house. A ground must be clearly made out before a seat can be lost, and the rules do not treat every political disagreement as a reason to remove a member. The grounds are set out in the Constitution and in the law itself, so the presiding officer applies a fixed checklist rather than an open-ended power. Membership of a legislature therefore depends on whether one of the listed grounds applies, and the booklet describes the grounds in some detail for this reason. When a listed ground is found to apply, the member can lose the seat. The booklet sets out these grounds one after another, so that each can be checked separately against the facts of a particular case. Each ground is a distinct condition, and a member is judged against the specific ground that has been alleged.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ground on which a legislator can be disqualified?
options: Criticising government policy in the House
Being declared of unsound mind by a court
questions.explanation: Being declared of unsound mind by a court is listed as a ground for disqualification.

questions.q: Which of these is a ground relating to a legislator's loyalty to the state?
questions.explanation: Showing allegiance to another country is listed as a ground, alongside losing Indian citizenship.

questions.q: Which of these is a ground for disqualification?
questions.explanation: Holding an office of profit is listed as a ground under Articles 102(1) and 191(1).

questions.q: Under any law made by which authority can a legislator be disqualified?
questions.explanation: Disqualification under any law made by Parliament is listed as a ground.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Being an undischarged insolvent is a ground for disqualification of a legislator.
Reason (R): The booklet lists being an undischarged insolvent among the grounds on which a legislator can be disqualified.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: R states the listed ground that makes A true.

questions.q:
Read the following statements:
I. Voluntarily giving up party membership is a ground for disqualification.
II. Abstaining from a vote contrary to the party whip is not a ground.
III. Disqualification under any law made by Parliament is a ground.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Abstaining contrary to the whip is a listed ground, so statement II is wrong.

questions.q:
Based on the booklet, how many of the following statements are correct?
I. Holding an office of profit is a ground for disqualification.
II. Being declared of unsound mind by a court is a ground for disqualification.
III. Criticising the party leadership in public is a ground for disqualification.
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are listed grounds, while criticising the party leadership is not among them.

quizzes.title: Grounds for Disqualification: typed-answer practice
quizzes.passage: A legislator can lose a seat only on grounds set out in a fixed list, not because of ordinary political disagreement. The list covers a member's conduct and personal circumstances. Some grounds concern choices a member makes in relation to a political party, such as conduct in the House. Other grounds concern the member's standing and legal position. Decisions on disqualification are taken by the presiding officer of the house, namely the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The presiding officer must establish that a ground applies before a seat is lost. The grounds are set out in the Constitution and in the law itself, so the presiding officer applies a fixed checklist rather than an open-ended power. Courts can review such decisions in certain circumstances, which is one reason the topic attracts attention. The booklet presents these grounds as a framework that governs when a member's place in the House is at risk. Each ground is a separate condition, and the presiding officer looks at the specific ground that has been alleged. The booklet sets out the grounds one after another, which makes it possible to check each one on its own terms. A member who is not caught by any listed ground keeps the seat, whatever the political disagreement may be.

questions.explanation: The booklet lists being an undischarged insolvent as a ground.

questions.q: A legislator declared of ___ mind by a court is liable to disqualification. (one word)
questions.explanation: Being declared of unsound mind by a court is a listed ground.

questions.q: Holding an office of ___ is a ground for disqualification. (one word)
questions.explanation: Holding an office of profit is a listed ground.

questions.q: Showing ___ to another country is a ground for disqualification. (one word)
questions.explanation: Showing allegiance to another country is a listed ground.

questions.q: Losing Indian ___ is a ground for disqualification. (one word)
questions.explanation: Losing Indian citizenship is a listed ground.

questions.q: A legislator can be disqualified under any law made by which body? (one word)
questions.explanation: Disqualification under any law made by Parliament is a listed ground.

questions.q: Voting or abstaining contrary to the party ___ is a ground for disqualification. (one word)
questions.explanation: Voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip is a listed ground.

quizzes.title: Significance and Key Issues: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage: Laws that govern elected members often attract debate, and the rules discussed here are part of that debate. The booklet looks at the purposes these rules serve and at the concerns that have been raised about how they work in practice. Presiding officers hold a central place in the framework, since they receive complaints and take the decisions that the rules require. Courts also form part of the picture, because their power to examine those decisions shapes how a matter is finally settled. Political parties are involved as well, since they issue instructions to their members in the legislature. The booklet treats several themes separately, and each one is presented with its supporting points. The rules are part of the Constitution itself. Taken together, these themes describe a framework that has clear strengths and also raises concerns on specific points. The discussion moves from the background of the rules to the way they work and then to the points on which they have been criticised. The framework is set out in a structured way, with its purpose, its working and its criticisms presented in turn. Each of these parts can be read on its own, and together they give a balanced account of the subject.

questions.q: Which key issue is linked to the two-thirds merger clause?
options: Rigid whip system on non-critical matters
Large-scale defections enabled by the merger clause
questions.explanation: The booklet says the two-thirds merger clause enables large-scale defections.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a significance of the Anti-Defection Law?
options: Abolishing the office of the Speaker
Making legislators accountable for their conduct
Allowing parties to be formed without members
questions.explanation: The booklet lists making legislators accountable for their conduct as a significance of the law.

questions.q: The law aims to prevent defections motivated by which of these?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the law prevents defections for office or material gain.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The rigid whip system is criticised for limiting intra-party democracy.
Reason (R): Party whips are issued even on matters that are not critical.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Whips issued on non-critical matters are the reason the booklet gives for reduced intra-party democracy.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Delay in decision-making   ->   A. Petitions pending for long durations
II. Allegations of bias   ->   B. Speaker or Chairman may act partisanly
III. Limited judicial intervention   ->   C. Courts intervene only after the Speaker's decision

questions.explanation: Each issue is matched with its description in the booklet: I-A, II-B, III-C, IV-D.

questions.q:
Read the following statements:
I. The law allows party mergers without disqualifying members.
II. Courts typically intervene before the Speaker decides a petition.
III. The rigid whip system is criticised for reducing intra-party democracy.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is wrong because courts typically intervene only after the Speaker's decision.

questions.q:
Based on the booklet, how many of the following statements are correct?
I. The law ensures party stability and prevents government instability.
II. The law makes legislators unaccountable for their conduct.
III. The law reinforces democracy and combats corruption.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are listed significances, while statement II reverses the booklet's point.

quizzes.title: Significance and Key Issues: typed-answer practice
quizzes.passage: Rules that govern elected members are often discussed in terms of their purpose and their effect on everyday politics. The booklet describes the framework as one that serves several functions, and it also records the concerns that critics have raised. The framework gives certain officers the job of deciding complaints, and those officers hold their posts within the legislature. Courts have a limited role, since they generally examine a matter only after the relevant officer has ruled on it. Party leaders issue instructions to members, and the booklet describes these instructions as applying in a wide range of situations. The merger provision is another point of discussion, since it allows members to act together in certain circumstances. The booklet also raises the question of how long complaints take to be resolved, which adds to the wider debate. Together these points give the reader a fuller view of how the framework works and why it attracts attention. The rules sit within the Constitution, which gives them a place among its provisions on the conduct of legislators. The booklet sets out the purposes of the framework, the officers who apply it, and the points on which it has drawn criticism, and these are discussed in turn. Several of the points are closely connected, so the reader is best served by seeing how they fit together.

questions.q: The law makes legislators ___ for their conduct. (one word)
